chapter.title: How should I act: Mill against Kant

cards.body: Mill and Kant sit on opposite sides of the table. Kant, speaking in 1785, says a right act is one whose rule everyone could follow. Mill, replying in 1861, says a right act is one that leaves the most people happiest. Nearly every argument about right and wrong since then has a guest leaning toward one of those two chairs.

cards.title: Two tests, two questions
cards.body:
Mill's test looks at results. An act is right if it produces the most happiness and the least suffering for everyone it affects, with each person counted once. This view is called utilitarianism, from 'utility', an old word for usefulness. You add up the good and the harm for everyone touched by the act, not just for yourself.

Kant's test looks at the rule behind the act. Before you act, state the rule you are following, such as 'break a promise when it suits me'. Then ask: could everyone act on that rule? If the rule would fall apart or wreck something once everyone followed it, the act is forbidden. Kant called this the categorical imperative: 'categorical' means no exceptions, 'imperative' means a command.

Kant gave a second way to say the same thing: never treat a person merely as a tool for your own purposes.

Notice the direction each test faces. Mill looks forward at what the act will cause. Kant looks down at the rule you are acting on right now.

options.text: Could everyone act on this rule?
Does this produce the most happiness for everyone affected?
Does this make me, the person acting, the happiest?

whyNot.a: That's Kant's test, not Mill's: Kant asks about the rule, Mill asks about the results.
whyNot.c: That's only half of Mill: he counts everyone the act touches, with each person counted once, not just you.

cards.reteach: Mill asks you to be an accountant. List every person the act affects, add up the happiness it gives them, subtract the suffering, and pick the act with the biggest total. Kant never does this sum. He asks whether the rule you are following could be followed by all.

cards.title: Dilemma 1: the false promise
cards.body:
Kant's own case from 1785: a man needs money and borrows it, promising to pay it back, while knowing he never will. Kant states his rule: 'make a false promise when I am in trouble.' Could everyone act on it? If they did, nobody would believe any promise, so promising itself would stop working. The rule destroys itself, so the act fails Kant's test.

Mill reaches the same verdict a different way. The lender loses his money, and every broken promise chips at the trust that lets strangers deal with each other. The harm to everyone outweighs the borrower's gain. On this dilemma the two tests agree.

cards.title: Where the tests split
cards.body:
Dilemma 2: your friend gives you a gift you dislike and asks if you love it. Mill counts: one small lie, one happy friend, nobody harmed, so the lie is probably right. He did warn that lies weaken trust, so the count is close. Kant states the rule 'lie when it is kinder' and asks if everyone could follow it. If they did, no compliment would mean anything. The rule collapses, so Kant says tell the truth.

Dilemma 3: someone who means to harm your friend knocks and asks where your friend is hiding. Kant wrote in 1797 that even here you must not lie. Mill says lie without a second thought, because one life weighs far more than one rule.

Most people side with Mill on dilemma 3. But Kant's test has a strength that shows up when the numbers point the other way. Mill's sum can justify hurting one person if enough others gain. Kant's rule forbids using a person merely as a tool, no matter how many benefit.

Neither test asks how you feel afterwards. Guilt or relief is a reaction, not a verdict.

cards.prompt: A town official can frame an innocent drifter for a crime, which would stop riots expected to kill several people. Run both tests. Which pair of verdicts is right?

options.text: Mill's test leans toward framing him, because fewer people die. Kant's test forbids it, because it uses him as a tool and the rule could not be followed by everyone.
Both tests forbid it, because both ask whether the rule could be followed by everyone.
Both tests allow it, because both add up the lives saved.

whyNot.b: That's Kant's question applied twice: Mill does not ask about the rule, he adds up results.
whyNot.c: That's Mill's sum applied twice: Kant never counts outcomes, so saved lives cannot tip his verdict.

cards.reteach: Picture the two thinkers at the door. Mill counts bodies on each side and picks the smaller pile, though his followers add that the long-run loss of trust might change his count. Kant ignores the piles and asks what the rule 'frame an innocent when it is useful' would do if everyone followed it. Different questions, so different answers.

cards.body: The common slip is to borrow one thinker's reason for the other thinker's verdict, such as 'Kant forbids lying because lying makes people unhappy.' That is Mill's reason wearing Kant's conclusion. Spot it fast: if the reason mentions results or happiness, it is Mill's test, whatever name is attached. If the reason mentions what would happen if everyone followed the rule, it is Kant's.

cards.prompt: You run a dilemma through both tests. What does each test ask?

options.text: Mill: could everyone act on this rule? Kant: does it produce the most happiness?
Mill: does it produce the most happiness for everyone affected? Kant: could everyone act on this rule?
Mill: does it make me happiest? Kant: would I feel guilty afterwards?

whyNot.a: That's the two tests swapped: Mill owns the happiness sum, Kant owns the everyone-rule.
whyNot.c: That's two things neither test asks: Mill counts everyone affected, not only you, and Kant asks about the rule, not your feelings.

cards.reteach: Keep one word per thinker. Mill: results. Kant: rule. Mill's question is about what the act will cause for everyone it touches. Kant's is about whether the rule behind the act could be everyone's rule.

cards.body: Tonight, pick one small choice you made today, such as a white lie or a shortcut. Write two lines: Mill's count of who gained and who lost, and Kant's rule stated as 'everyone does this when...'.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now run one moral dilemma through Mill's happiness test and Kant's everyone-rule test and say where they give different answers.
